newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia PM to push free trade during Clinton trip.
newsitem.headline: Australia PM to push free trade during Clinton trip.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard, declaring a shared Asia-Pacific future with the United States, said on Monday he would seek President Bill Clinton's continued support for freer world trade in talks this week.
In a series of interviews published on the eve of Clinton's first Australian visit, Howard said trade would figure heavily in a meeting between the two leaders here on Wednesday.
But Australia's opposition and the country's main national daily newspaper both called on Howard to raise with Clinton the issue of Chinese engagement in the region.

Howard's conservative Liberal-National government has pledged to reinvigorate ties with Washington, a long-term ally, saying the former Labor government ignored the important relationship in favour of closer ties with Asia.
But China has expressed concern over Australia's closer links with Washington, which include stronger defence ties, claiming it is part of an unofficial U.S. policy of containment.

On Monday, Howard said he would seek Clinton's backing to maintain the momentum for trade liberalisation, ahead of a key Asia-Pacific economic summit next Monday. Clinton arrives in Australia on Tuesday for a five-day trip.

"The main thing I will be putting to him -- I think it will fall on very fertile ground -- is that we need to keep up the momentum towards trade liberalisation," Howard told the Australian Financial Review newspaper.
Howard told a Liberal party gathering on Sunday that Australia's economic and political future was irrevocably tied to the booming Asian region.
But he added that the U.S. and Australia shared a long and close relationship and there was "a shared destiny and future of Australia and the United States in the Asian-Pacific region".
"It is, of course, a relationship that goes beyond formal defence and treaty ties," Howard said.

"It is a relationship forged out of a common cultural inheritance, a common commitment to liberty, a common pursuit of the defence of freedom and a shared belief that the values of our two societies are important and are worth fighting for and worth defending," he said.
Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley has urged Howard to discuss with Clinton the issue of engagement of China.
Beazley said he would raise the need to involve China "effectively in a security dialogue" when he met Clinton.
Sino-Australian relations have chilled under Howard's administration over a range of security and diplomatic issues.

"Most of our neighbours understand that keeping America fully engaged in Asia is one of the key strategic challenges of the decade, and they are at ease with the U.S. and Australian positions," said The Australian newspaper in an editorial on Monday.

"But China is another matter. Its perception is that....Washington is using Japan and Australia as...anchors of an encirclement of China that respresents a potential threat to China's interests in the region," the newspaper said.
"This Chinese perception is something that Mr Howard and Mr Clinton need to review comprehensively..."
The Clinton-Howard talks come ahead of next week's summit of Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) forum leaders, which will discuss the group's pact to axe trade barriers by 2020.
Both leaders are scheduled to meet China's president Jiang Zemin at the APEC summit.

APEC groups Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and the United States.
